q.q: What is the main purpose of system software?
o: To help the user carry out one particular task
To let the user write reports and edit photos
To run and manage the computer and its hardware
To meet the exact needs of one organisation
q.why: System software controls the hardware and provides a platform for other programs. Helping with a task is application software.

q.q: Which of these is system software?
o: A web browser such as Chrome
A device driver for a printer
A photo editor such as Photoshop
A school management information system
q.why: Device drivers let the OS talk to hardware, so they are system software. The others help the user do a task.

q.q: A web browser comes already installed on a new laptop. Why is it still application software?
o: It helps the user do a task rather than keeping the computer running
It is loaded first, straight from ROM, whenever the computer starts
It controls the hardware and shares out memory and processor time
It is stored with the operating system, so it is part of the system
q.why: Coming pre-installed does not matter: a browser helps the user do a task, so it is an application.

q.q: Which statement about application software is true?
o: It can run on its own without any other software underneath it
It relies on the operating system to load it and give it processor time
It is loaded automatically from ROM as soon as the power comes on
It manages the memory and storage used by all other programs
q.why: Applications need the OS to load them into memory, give them processor time and save their files.

q.q: Which is the most important example of system software?
o: The operating system
A word processor
A backup utility
A printer driver
q.why: The OS is the main piece of system software. Utilities and drivers are also system software but less central; a word processor is an application.

q.q: Which describes packaged (off-the-shelf) software?
o: Written for one organisation, so it fits their way of working exactly
Made for many users, so it takes months to design, write and test
Made for many users with similar needs, so it is cheap and available at once
Written for one user, so it is cheap and well supported by forums
q.why: Packaged software serves many users, so costs are shared and it is ready immediately with plenty of support.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of tailored software compared with packaged software?
o: It does not fit the way the organisation actually works
It has to be bought ready-made from a shop or website
It costs much more and takes months to design, write and test
It cannot be updated once it has been installed
q.why: Bespoke software fits exactly but is expensive and slow to produce.

q.q: A small café needs a program to keep track of its weekly takings. Which is most suitable?
o: Tailored software, because it is cheap and available straight away
System software, because it manages the café's financial data
Tailored software, because it has more guides and online forums
Packaged software, because it is cheap and available straight away
q.why: A common, simple job suits off-the-shelf software, which is cheap, ready now and well supported.

q.q: Which pair gives an example of system software followed by an example of application software?
o: Excel, then Windows 11
Chrome, then Photoshop
Android, then a device driver
Windows 11, then Excel
q.why: Windows 11 is an operating system; Excel helps the user do a task. Android and a device driver are both system software.

q.q: Who does application software serve directly?
o: The hardware
The user
The operating system
Device drivers
q.why: Applications help the user directly; system software serves the hardware and other programs.

q.q: Where must a program be before the processor can run it?
o: In ROM
In main memory (RAM)
On the storage drive only
In a backup
q.why: The processor only works on programs and data held in main memory, so the OS copies programs into RAM.

q.q: When a program is closed, what does the operating system do with the memory it was using?
o: Copies it into ROM so the program starts faster next time
Locks the space so no other program can ever use it
Defragments it so the program is stored in one block
Releases the space so it can be used by something else
q.why: Freeing memory on close lets the space be allocated to other programs.

q.q: Why does the operating system keep programs apart in memory?
o: So one program cannot overwrite another program's data
So programs can share each other's data more easily
So each program can run from ROM instead of RAM
So the processor can run every program at the same instant
q.why: The OS records which program owns which part of memory and protects each area.

q.q: A pupil has dozens of browser tabs open and the computer slows down. What is the most likely reason?
o: The processor has been given too many time slices by the operating system
RAM is full, so the OS is using slower virtual memory on the storage drive
The storage drive is being defragmented automatically in the background
ROM is full, so the start-up instructions keep having to be reloaded
q.why: When RAM fills up the OS borrows part of the storage drive as virtual memory, which is much slower.

q.q: Which is a storage-management job of the operating system?
o: Giving each running task a short time slice of processor time
Copying programs from the storage drive into RAM to run them
Checking that the hardware works when the computer is switched on
Controlling who may read or change each file using permissions
q.why: Storage management saves files, records locations, frees space and sets permissions. Time slices are processor management; loading into RAM is memory management.

q.q: A pupil sees 'Access denied' when opening a folder on a shared drive. Which OS function caused this?
o: Storage management controlling file permissions
Memory management protecting areas of RAM
Processor management handing out time slices
The boot-up sequence checking the hardware
q.why: The OS controls who may read or change each file, so it blocked access to that folder.

q.q: What is a time slice?
o: A section of RAM given to a program while it is running
A block of storage where part of a file is saved
A tiny amount of processor time given to a task in turn
The time the computer takes to finish starting up
q.why: The OS splits processor time into tiny slices and hands them to each running task in turn.

q.q: Music keeps playing while a pupil types an essay. Which OS function makes this possible?
o: Allocating storage space for the music files
Allocating processing time in time slices
Allocating memory to the essay as virtual memory
Loading device drivers during start-up
q.why: Switching the processor between tasks thousands of times a second is multitasking, so both seem to run at once.

q.q: Which tasks does the operating system give more time slices to?
o: Tasks with a higher priority, such as responding to the mouse
Tasks that use the most storage space on the drive
Tasks that were the first to start when the computer booted
Tasks that have been running for the longest time so far
q.why: Higher-priority tasks receive more slices so the computer stays responsive.

q.q: A processor core can carry out only one instruction at a time. Why do several programs seem to run at once?
o: The OS switches between them thousands of times a second
Each program runs on its own copy of the operating system
The core secretly carries out several instructions together
The programs take turns to run from ROM instead of RAM
q.why: Rapid switching between time slices makes the programs appear to run together (multitasking).

q.q: Why are the start-up instructions stored in ROM?
o: ROM is volatile, so it is empty and ready to be filled at switch-on
ROM is larger than the storage drive, so it can hold the whole OS
ROM is faster than RAM, so the operating system runs from it
ROM is non-volatile, so the instructions are there when the power comes on
q.why: The first instructions must be in memory the moment power arrives; ROM keeps its contents when switched off.

q.q: Why can RAM not hold the very first instructions run at switch-on?
o: RAM is volatile, so it is empty when the computer is switched on
RAM is too small to hold even a few start-up instructions
RAM can only hold data, not program instructions
RAM is read-only, so new instructions cannot be added
q.why: RAM loses its contents when the power is off, so it is empty at switch-on.

q.q: What is the power-on self-test (POST)?
o: A check that key hardware such as memory and drives is present and working
A program that copies the core of the OS from storage into RAM
The order in which storage devices are searched for an operating system
The log-in screen shown once the operating system has taken control
q.why: POST is the step where the start-up instructions test the hardware.

q.q: How is a hardware fault found during the self-test usually reported?
o: By emailing the network manager automatically
With an on-screen message or a series of beeps
By removing the operating system from storage
By starting a full antivirus scan straight away
q.why: The firmware reports faults with a message or beeps before the OS is loaded.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the boot-up sequence?
o: ROM instructions run, hardware tested, OS found, OS loaded into RAM
Hardware tested, ROM instructions run, OS loaded into RAM, OS found
ROM instructions run, OS loaded into RAM, hardware tested, OS found
OS found, ROM instructions run, hardware tested, OS loaded into RAM
q.why: The ROM firmware runs first, tests the hardware, finds the OS on storage and loads it into RAM.

q.q: Why is the operating system itself not stored in ROM?
o: ROM loses its contents when switched off
The processor cannot read from ROM at all
ROM can only store data and never programs
It is too large and changes too often
q.why: The OS stays on the storage drive until it is loaded because it is big and frequently updated.

q.q: During boot-up, what does the small loader program do?
o: Copies the core of the operating system from storage into RAM
Tests the memory, keyboard and storage drives for faults
Copies the start-up instructions from RAM back into ROM
Shows the log-in screen and opens the user's files
q.why: The loader moves the OS core into RAM so the processor can run it.

q.q: What happens in the final 'hand over' step of the boot-up sequence?
o: The firmware looks through the storage devices to find an operating system
The processor runs the start-up instructions that are stored in ROM
The hardware is checked and any faults are reported with a series of beeps
The OS takes control, loads drivers and services, and shows the log-in screen
q.why: Once loaded into RAM, the OS takes over, loads device drivers and background services, and shows the log-in screen.

q.q: How does the firmware decide which storage device to load the OS from?
o: It always picks the device with the most free space
It looks through the devices in a set boot order
It asks the user to choose a device every time
It picks whichever device was installed most recently
q.why: The firmware searches storage devices in a set boot order to find one holding an OS.

q.q: Which statement about the boot-up sequence is INCORRECT?
o: The start-up firmware is often called the BIOS or UEFI
The OS is copied into RAM before it takes control
Key hardware is checked before the OS is loaded
The boot program is stored in RAM so it is ready at switch-on
q.why: The boot program is in ROM, not RAM; RAM is empty at switch-on. This was a common slip reported by the Chief Examiner.

q.q: What is the defining feature of real-time processing?
o: Data is collected over time and processed together later
Output is produced quickly enough to affect the next input
Many users share one processor using short time slices
Data is processed overnight without people taking part
q.why: Speed alone is not enough: the result must be ready in time to affect the next input.

q.q: When a fan buys a concert seat at the SSE Arena, the seat is marked as sold immediately. Why does this matter?
o: The seat can be added to the next overnight batch run
The fan's bill can be produced at the end of the month
The transaction file can be matched to the master file
The next customer sees it as taken, so it cannot be sold twice
q.why: Real-time updating means the next input (another customer) sees the correct seat plan.

q.q: Which is an example of real-time processing?
o: Producing quarterly gas bills
Traffic lights responding to sensors
Running monthly payroll for a council
Printing monthly bank statements
q.why: Traffic lights must react at once to each input. The others are classic batch jobs.

q.q: Which describes batch processing?
o: Each item of data is processed the moment it is entered into the system
Similar data is collected over time and processed together later without people
Many users at separate terminals share one powerful central processor
Data is processed instantly so that the files are always fully up to date
q.why: Batch groups similar data and processes it all together later, unattended.

q.q: Why are batch runs often scheduled overnight or at weekends?
o: Batch processing needs staff to supervise each record as it runs
Data entered during the day is not accurate until the evening
The computer cannot do other work while a big batch is running
Real-time processing can only take place during working hours
q.why: A large batch ties up the computer, so it is run when the computer is quiet.

q.q: In a batch billing system, what does the master file hold?
o: Only the new meter readings that have been collected during this quarter
The finished bills that are ready to be posted out to every customer
Permanent customer details such as account number, name and previous reading
A temporary list of readings that is deleted once each bill is printed
q.why: The master file is permanent; the new readings go in the temporary transaction file.

q.q: During a batch billing run, how is each new reading matched to the right customer?
o: By the customer's surname
By the date of the reading
By the account number
By the customer's address
q.why: Each transaction is matched to the master record with the same account number, which is unique.

q.q: What is produced at the end of a batch billing run, ready for the next quarter?
o: A new transaction file holding the old readings
A new master file holding the new readings
A copy of the first transaction only
A list of customers who paid in real time
q.why: The run writes a new master file with the new readings, ready for next time.

q.q: Which task is LEAST suited to batch processing?
o: Producing utility bills each quarter
Running a company's monthly payroll
Producing monthly bank statements
Online stock control as items are sold
q.why: Stock must be updated at once for the next sale, so it needs real-time processing.

q.q: Why does the answer 'real-time means fast' not earn the mark?
o: Real-time processing is actually slower than batch processing
Real-time processing normally takes place overnight when quiet
Speed is a feature of batch processing rather than real-time
It does not say the output is ready in time to affect the next input
q.why: Examiners want the defining idea: output produced in time to affect the next input, linked to the scenario.

q.q: What is a multi-user system?
o: One user runs several programs on one computer at the same time
Data from many users is collected and processed together later on
Each user has their own separate computer that is not connected
Many users at different terminals share the processor of one central computer
q.why: Multi-user (time-sharing) means many terminals share one powerful processor.

q.q: What is another name for a multi-user system?
o: Batch system
Multitasking system
Real-time system
Time-sharing system
q.why: Processor time is shared between users, so it is a time-sharing system. Multitasking is one user running several programs.

q.q: What is the round robin method?
o: Giving the most time to the user who logged on first
Giving each user a separate processor of their own
Giving all users the processor at exactly the same time
Giving each user a time slice in turn in a fixed circle
q.why: After the last user, the OS returns to the first and continues in a circle.

q.q: Why does each user of a time-sharing system feel they have the computer to themselves?
o: Each user is given a processor core of their own to work with
The OS gives every user the whole processor at the same time
Each turn comes round very quickly because the processor is so fast
Each user's work is saved and processed later in a batch run
q.why: Billions of instructions a second mean each user's turn returns almost at once.

q.q: 8 users each get a 20 ms time slice. How long is one full round?
o: 160 ms
28 ms
180 ms
2.5 ms
q.why: One round is 8 × 20 = 160 ms. Adding (28) or dividing (2.5) are common slips.

q.q: In a round robin system, one full round of 10 terminals takes 50 ms. How long is each time slice?
o: 500 ms
60 ms
5 ms
40 ms
q.why: Each slice = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 ms.

q.q: How does multi-user processing differ from multitasking?
o: Multi-user is one user running several programs; multitasking is many people sharing one processor
Multi-user processes data overnight later; multitasking processes each item as it arrives
Multi-user is many people sharing one processor; multitasking is one user running several programs
They are two different names for exactly the same way of sharing a processor
q.why: The notes stress the difference: multi-user = many users; multitasking = one user, several programs.

q.q: Which is an example of a multi-user system?
o: Pupils logging on to a shared school server
Producing exam result slips overnight
One pupil running music and a word processor
A gas company producing quarterly bills
q.why: Many pupils share central servers at once. One pupil running two programs is multitasking.

q.q: An airline booking system is both real-time and multi-user. Which explains why?
o: Many bookings are collected and then processed together overnight
Many agents use it at once, and each booking updates the seat plan instantly
One agent runs several programs while each booking waits its turn
Bookings are held in a transaction file until the end of the month
q.why: Multi-user describes many people sharing it; real-time describes each booking being processed at once.

q.q: Which statement correctly compares real-time and multi-user processing?
o: Real-time is about how one processor is shared; multi-user is about how quickly inputs are processed
Real-time is always run as a batch; a multi-user system can never be real-time
Real-time is about how quickly inputs are processed; multi-user is about how one processor is shared
Real-time needs many users at once; a multi-user system needs only a single user
q.why: They describe different things, which is why one system can be both.

q.q: A sports centre lets people book badminton courts online. Which mode and justification is best?
o: Real-time, so availability changes instantly and a court cannot be double-booked
Batch, so all of the bookings can be processed together overnight
Batch, because there is a large volume of similar booking records
Real-time, because it is the newest and most modern method
q.why: A delay would allow double bookings, so real-time is needed. 'Newest' is not a context-linked reason.

q.q: A school must produce exam result slips for a whole year group. Which mode and reason fit best?
o: Real-time, because each slip must affect the next input
Batch, because every slip is produced the same way at one fixed time
Multi-user, because many pupils will read the slips
Real-time, because results must appear the moment they are typed
q.why: Many similar outputs needed at a set time are ideal for batch processing.

q.q: Why should supermarket tills update stock using real-time processing?
o: Stock data is a large volume that can wait until the end of the month
Stock levels must be correct for the next sale and for online orders
The tills are only used when the computer is quiet during the night
The tills each run several programs on their own at the same time
q.why: A wrong stock level would affect the very next sale, so updates cannot wait.

q.q: Which question points you towards choosing real-time processing?
o: Is there a large amount of similar data needed at set times?
Do many people need the same central system at once?
Would a delay cause a problem such as a double booking?
Can the job run unattended when the computer is free?
q.why: A delay causing errors or danger signals real-time. The other questions point to batch or multi-user.

q.q: Which is the strongest justification for using batch processing for a council's payroll?
o: It is the cheapest mode for any organisation and easy for staff to set up
Each payslip updates the moment a worker clocks in, so pay is always exact
Many similar records; pay only needed at month end; can run overnight unattended
Many staff can log on to see their payslips at the same time every day
q.why: A strong batch answer mentions volume of similar data, a fixed time and unattended running.

q.q: A school network lets hundreds of pupils log in to central servers at the same time. Which mode of processing is this?
o: Batch
Multitasking
Multi-user
Embedded
q.why: Many users sharing central servers at once is multi-user. Multitasking is one user running several programs.

q.q: Why would batch processing be unsuitable for selling cinema seats?
o: Seats would not be updated until later, so one seat could be sold twice
Batch would update every seat at once and waste processor time
Batch processing cannot cope with more than one cinema screen
Batch processing needs each customer to attend the overnight run
q.why: With batch, availability is out of date until the run, so double bookings could happen.

q.q: A leisure centre sends renewal letters to all members each month and takes class bookings online. Which pairing is best?
o: Real-time for the renewal letters; batch for the class bookings
Batch for both, run overnight at the end of each week
Multi-user for the letters; batch for the class bookings
Batch for the renewal letters; real-time for the class bookings
q.why: Letters are high-volume and needed at a set time (batch); bookings must update at once (real-time).

q.q: In a 6-mark 'discuss' question on modes of processing, what is a good way to show depth?
o: Naming a mode for every task without giving reasons
Listing as many modes of processing as you can
Saying real-time is fast while batch is slow
Explaining why the other mode would be unsuitable for the task
q.why: The top band needs context-linked reasons; saying why the other mode would fail shows depth.

q.q: An electricity company sends a bill to every customer each quarter. Why is batch processing suitable?
o: Each customer must see their bill change the moment they use power
A large volume of similar data is only needed at a set time
Each customer needs a terminal connected to the central computer
Each bill must be ready in time to affect the next meter reading
q.why: Quarterly bills are many similar records needed at a fixed time, so they can wait for a batch run.

q.q: What is utility software?
o: Application software that helps the user carry out a task such as writing
Tailored software that has been written for one particular organisation
Firmware stored in ROM that runs each time the computer is switched on
System software that does one specific job to keep the computer fast, tidy and safe
q.why: Utilities are small system programs that maintain, protect or speed up the computer.

q.q: What does a disk defragmenter do?
o: Deletes temporary files to free up space on the disk
Copies files to a separate place in case they are lost
Moves the pieces of each file together and gathers the free space
Scans files and removes any viruses it finds
q.why: Defragmenting rejoins file fragments and groups free space. Deleting temporary files is disk clean-up.

q.q: What are the two jobs of a task scheduler?
o: Sharing memory between programs and deleting temporary files
Sharing processor time between tasks and running jobs at set times
Moving file fragments together and grouping the free space
Copying data to a backup and restoring it after a loss
q.why: It keeps the processor busy (round robin in multi-user systems) and runs jobs automatically at set times.

q.q: A network manager wants updates to install automatically whenever computers shut down. Which utility sets this up?
o: Disk defragmenter
Backup
Task scheduler
Restore
q.why: Running jobs at a set time or when an event happens is a task-scheduling job.

q.q: What is a backup?
o: The original data moved into a new folder
A copy of data stored separately from the original
A record of where each file is stored on disk
A compressed version kept in the same place
q.why: A backup is a separate copy, so it survives if the original is lost.

q.q: What does it mean to restore data?
o: Making a new copy of the data and storing it off-site
Moving each file's blocks so they are next to each other
Copying backed-up data back to return the system to an earlier state
Isolating an infected file so that it cannot run
q.why: Restore uses the backup copy to recover lost data.

q.q: In a multi-user system, which method does the task scheduler use to share processor time?
o: Batch processing
Virtual memory
Quarantine
Round robin
q.why: Each terminal gets a time slice in turn: the round robin method.

q.q: What is a benefit of using the task scheduler for backups and virus scans?
o: Jobs run when nobody is using the system and are never forgotten
Jobs run while users are working so they can watch progress
Scheduled jobs take up less storage space than manual ones
Scheduled jobs never need to be checked or tested afterwards
q.why: Automatic scheduling means maintenance always happens, at quiet times.

q.q: Which utility deletes temporary files to free up disk space?
o: Disk defragmenter
Task scheduler
Restore
Disk clean-up
q.why: Disk clean-up removes temporary files. A defragmenter rearranges files but does not delete them.

q.q: Why would 'it tidies up the disk' not score a mark for defragmenting?
o: Defragmenting does not change the layout of the disk in any way
Defragmenting only tidies the computer's RAM, not the disk
Defragmenting is really a job done by the task scheduler
It does not say what is moved, where, and why it makes access faster
q.why: A good answer says the fragments of each file are moved next to each other, giving faster access.

q.q: Before a file is saved, the operating system splits it into…
o: equal-sized data blocks
variable-sized fragments
separate time slices
individual folders
q.why: Files are split into equal-sized blocks, which go into free block spaces on the disk.

q.q: Why does file fragmentation happen?
o: Viruses split files into pieces and spread them across the disk
The disk spins more slowly as it gets older and more worn
Files are compressed every time they are saved to the disk
Deleting and editing files leaves scattered gaps, so large new files are split
q.why: Free space becomes many small gaps; a large file that fits no single gap is stored in pieces.

q.q: Why does a fragmented file open slowly on a hard disk drive?
o: The file becomes larger once it has been split up into many separate blocks
The read/write head must jump to many places and wait for the platter to spin round
The processor must decompress each fragment before the file can be opened
RAM has to store every fragment twice before the file can be opened
q.why: Each extra head movement takes milliseconds, which slows opening and saving.

q.q: When does fragmentation tend to get worse?
o: The fuller and older the disk is
The newer and emptier the disk is
The smaller the files that are saved
The more RAM the computer has
q.why: Months of saving and deleting on a fuller disk leave more scattered gaps.

q.q: Why should a solid-state drive (SSD) not be defragmented?
o: It has no moving parts, so it gains nothing, and extra writes wear it out
SSDs do not store files as blocks, so they cannot become fragmented
SSDs automatically delete any file that has become fragmented
SSDs are always too full for the defragmenter to move any blocks
q.why: Scattered blocks are read just as quickly on an SSD, and needless writing shortens its life.

q.q: After defragmenting, why can new files be saved without being split?
o: The free space has been gathered into one area
Every file has been compressed to save space
The hard disk has been changed into an SSD
Old files have been moved into the backup
q.why: Grouping the free space leaves a large continuous area for new files.

q.q: Which answer fully explains fragmentation and defragmentation (cause, effect and fix)?
o: Files are split up by viruses, so the disk spins more slowly; defragmenting removes the viruses, so access is faster again
Files are split into blocks stored together, so RAM fills up; defragmenting adds more RAM, so the access is faster
Files are copied many times, so the disk becomes full; defragmenting deletes the copies, so more storage is freed
Files are split into blocks stored where space is free, so the head moves more; defragmenting moves blocks together, so access is faster
q.why: A full answer gives the cause (blocks stored wherever space is free), the effect (more head movement) and the fix (blocks moved together).

q.q: On an eight-block disk, File A uses blocks 1, 2 and 3, and File B uses blocks 4, 6 and 8. Blocks 5 and 7 are free. Which statement is correct?
o: File B is fragmented because its blocks are not next to each other
File A is fragmented because it starts at the first block
Both files are fragmented because there are free blocks
Neither file is fragmented because each uses three blocks
q.why: File A is in one continuous run; File B's blocks are separated by gaps.

q.q: Which of these is a result of defragmenting a hard disk?
o: Each file is compressed losslessly to save space
Each file is copied to off-site storage for safety
Each file's blocks are stored next to each other, in order
Each file is scanned against a list of virus signatures
q.why: Defragmenting rearranges blocks; it does not compress, back up or scan files.

q.q: What does a full backup copy?
o: Only the data changed since the last backup
Only the operating system files
All of the data every time
Only the files the user has opened today
q.why: A full backup copies everything; copying only changes is an incremental backup.

q.q: What is an advantage of a full backup over an incremental backup?
o: It is quicker to restore because everything is in one place
It takes less time to make each night
It needs much less storage space
It copies only the files that changed
q.why: Full backups are slow and large, but restoring needs just one backup set.

q.q: What is an advantage of an incremental backup over a full backup?
o: Restoring needs only one backup set
It copies all the data every time
It removes the need for any full backup
It is much faster to make and needs less storage
q.why: Copying only changes makes it quick and small, though restoring is more work.

q.q: A full backup is taken on Sunday and incremental backups Monday to Friday. The disk fails on Saturday morning. What is needed to restore?
o: Sunday's full backup and Friday's incremental backup only
Friday's incremental backup only, because it is the newest
Sunday's full backup, then the Monday to Friday incrementals in order
The Monday to Friday incrementals only, newest first
q.why: Each incremental holds only that day's changes, so all are applied in order after the full backup.

q.q: Why should several generations of backups be kept?
o: So each backup takes up less storage space
So you can go back to before a file was corrupted
So each night's backup runs more quickly
So no off-site copy of the data is needed
q.why: If corruption is copied into the latest backup, an older generation still has the good version.

q.q: Why should restoring from backups be tested regularly?
o: Testing makes the next backup run faster
A backup that cannot be restored is useless
Testing removes the need for a full backup
Testing defragments the backup drive
q.why: The whole point of a backup is recovery, so it must be shown to work.

q.q: Why are backups usually scheduled to run overnight?
o: Data saved during the day is not accurate until the night
Backups can only be made when the screens are turned off
Incremental backups can only start after midnight
The network is quiet, so the backup does not slow users down
q.why: Running when the network is quiet avoids slowing down users.

q.q: How often might a real-time system need to back up?
o: Possibly after every transaction, because the data changes so often
Once a month, because the data in it hardly ever changes
Only after a disk has failed and the data has been lost
Once a year, using a single full backup of the whole system
q.why: Data that changes often needs backing up often; real-time systems may back up after every transaction.

q.q: Which is the most suitable backup procedure for a school?
o: Full backup weekly to the same drive as the data, run by hand during lessons
Full backup weekly, incrementals on other nights, scheduled overnight, copies kept off-site
Incremental backups every night but never a full backup, kept in the server room
Full backup once a year, kept in the office next to the server it was made from
q.why: A good procedure combines full and incremental backups, runs automatically when quiet and stores copies off-site.

q.q: A full backup on Sunday uses 40 GB and each incremental on Monday to Saturday uses 2 GB. How much storage does the week need?
o: 52 GB
42 GB
54 GB
280 GB
q.why: 40 + (6 × 2) = 52 GB. 280 GB would be seven full backups.

q.q: A school's server room floods. Why does an off-site backup help?
o: The backup stops the flood water damaging the server
The backup is quicker to make when it is stored off-site
The backup is not destroyed along with the original data
The backup can be restored without needing a full backup
q.why: Storing copies elsewhere means one disaster cannot destroy both the original and the backup.

q.q: What is a computer virus?
o: A file whose blocks have been stored in separate places across the disk
A program that copies data to a separate place to keep it safe
A file that has been isolated so that it cannot run or spread
A harmful program that attaches to a file and copies itself when the file is opened
q.why: A virus runs when its host file is opened and spreads to other files and computers.

q.q: What is a virus signature?
o: The name of the person who wrote the virus
The date a virus was first found on a computer
A pattern of code that identifies a particular known virus
A password needed to remove a virus safely
q.why: Antivirus software compares files with a database of these code patterns.

q.q: What does heuristic checking by antivirus software look for?
o: Files whose code exactly matches a known virus signature
Files that have been split into many separate fragments
Programs acting suspiciously, such as rapidly altering many files
Files that are larger than a set size limit for the drive
q.why: Behaviour checking can flag a brand-new virus that has no signature yet. Exact matching is signature checking.

q.q: What is real-time protection?
o: Scanning the whole disk once a week at a set time
Updating the signature database once a month
Scanning files automatically as they are opened or downloaded
Backing up files as soon as they are changed
q.why: Real-time protection checks each file as it is opened, as well as scheduled full scans.

q.q: Why might antivirus software fail to detect a brand-new virus using signature checking?
o: It is stored on a USB stick
Its signature is not yet in the database
It has already been quarantined
The disk has just been defragmented
q.why: Signature checking only recognises viruses whose signatures are already in the database.

q.q: What is the best practice for antivirus updates?
o: Download them automatically at least once a day
Download them by hand at the end of each month
Download them only after a virus has been found
Download them once a year when the licence renews
q.why: New viruses appear daily, so signatures must be updated automatically and often.

q.q: An antivirus program finds an infected file that it cannot repair. What keeps the file from causing harm without deleting it?
o: Moving it to quarantine
Running a restore
Defragmenting the disk
Scheduling a backup
q.why: Quarantine is an isolated area where infected files cannot run or spread.

q.q: Apart from adding new virus signatures, why else are antivirus updates important?
o: They defragment the disk so that scans run faster
They make a backup of every file before scanning
They fix weaknesses in the antivirus program itself
They speed up the boot-up sequence at switch-on
q.why: Updates also patch weaknesses in the antivirus software.

q.q: A youth club leader plugs in a USB stick from home. What should the antivirus software do?
o: Defragment the stick before any of its files are opened
Scan the stick when it is connected, before files are opened
Back up the stick to the cloud before it is scanned
Restore the stick to an earlier state straight away
q.why: Antivirus scans connected storage, comparing files with signatures before they can run.

q.q: Which pair of points fully answers 'Why must antivirus software be updated regularly?'
o: New viruses are created all the time, and updates make the computer start up more quickly
New viruses are created all the time, and only viruses whose signatures it holds can be detected
Old viruses become stronger over time, and updates restore any files that were deleted
Old signatures take up storage space, and updates delete them to free space on the disk
q.why: Both halves are needed: new viruses keep appearing and signature checking only finds known ones.
